Where a Snapchat purchase event dies

The customer journey from ad click to Snapchat Events Manager, with the six failure causes marked beneath the stage where each one occurs: pixel re-initialisation at checkout, session loss at the payment gateway, lowercase event name, missing transaction ID and missing pixel at the confirmation page, and deduplication at Snapchat.

<t0>The confirmation page is where most of it goes wrong.</t0> Three of the six causes bite at the final step, which is also the step people test least, because testing it properly means spending real money.

Snapchat tracking gets far less written about than Meta or Google, which means when it breaks you are mostly on your own. The articles that do exist tend to be written by companies selling a tracking product, so they stop at "install our app." This is the sequence I actually run, in the order I run it, and why that order.
First: confirm the event genuinely isn't arriving
Before changing anything, establish whether the event is missing or merely delayed. Two checks, sixty seconds.

<t0>Check the network, not the dashboard.</t0> Open your confirmation page in Chrome, open DevTools (F12), go to the <t1>Network</t1> tab, and filter for <t2>tr.snapchat.com</t2>. Complete a real test purchase. If you see a request fire with your pixel ID and the event name, the browser is doing its job and your problem is downstream, reporting, deduplication, or attribution. If nothing fires, the problem is on the page.

The <t0>Snap Pixel Helper</t0> browser extension does the same job with a friendlier interface, and will also tell you whether the pixel is installed at all. I use the Network tab because it shows the exact payload, and the payload is usually where the answer is.

<t0>If the first three appear and the fourth doesn't, your problem is on the confirmation page.</t0> If none of them appear, the pixel isn't installed where you think it is.
<t0>Give it time before you panic</t0>

Events Manager reporting is not instant. Before concluding an event is missing, wait a few hours and re-check. I have watched people rewrite a working checkout because they looked at a dashboard ninety seconds after a test order.
The six causes, ranked
The event name is lowercase

Snapchat's standard events are <t0>uppercase</t0>: <t1>PURCHASE</t1>, <t2>ADD_CART</t2>, <t3>PAGE_VIEW</t3>, <t4>START_CHECKOUT</t4>. If you send <t5>purchase</t5>, it is not recognised as a standard event. The insidious part is that it may still fire and still appear somewhere, it simply won't be treated as the standard conversion, so campaign optimisation and reporting behave as though nothing happened.

This is number one because it produces the exact symptom people describe, "the pixel is firing but Events Manager shows nothing", and because copying a Meta implementation across is a natural thing to do. Meta uses <t0>Purchase</t0>. Snapchat does not.
✗ Ported from Meta
✓ What Snapchat expects
<t0>The check</t0>In the Network tab, read the event name in the request payload. It must be exactly <t1>PURCHASE</t1>. Capitalisation is not cosmetic here.
No transaction_id is being sent

Without <t0>transaction_id</t0>, Snapchat has no way to tell a genuine second order from the same customer refreshing the confirmation page. Snap documents a <t1>30-day deduplication window</t1> on <t2>transaction_id</t2>, versus 48 hours for <t3>client_dedup_id</t3>.

The failure mode cuts both ways, which is why it belongs this high. Omit it and refreshes inflate your purchase count. Send a value that isn't actually unique per order (a cart ID, a checkout ID, a session ID) and legitimate orders get collapsed into one and <t0>vanish</t0>. The second case looks exactly like "my events aren't firing."
<t0>The check</t0>Place two test orders. Confirm the <t1>transaction_id</t1> differs between them, and that it matches the order number your store actually assigns.
The pixel isn't on the page that actually confirms the order

Almost everyone installs the pixel sitewide and assumes the confirmation page inherits it. Frequently it doesn't. Hosted checkouts, order-status pages and post-purchase upsell flows are often rendered outside the theme or template that carries your tracking code.
Worth checking specifically: if you run a post-purchase upsell, the page a customer lands on immediately after paying may not be the page you think of as the thank-you page.
<t0>The check</t0>Complete a real order. On the page you land on, view source and search for your pixel ID. Do not infer it from the theme, look at the page the customer is actually on.
An off-site payment redirect breaks the session

When checkout hands off to an external gateway and returns the customer to an order-received page, that round trip can break the browser session the pixel depends on. The purchase completes, the customer sees their confirmation, and the event never reaches Snapchat, or arrives stripped of the identifiers needed to attribute it.

This is the point where a browser-only setup stops being sufficient. Server-side tracking via the <t0>Conversions API</t0> is the durable fix, because the event originates from your server and never depends on surviving a redirect.
<t0>The check</t0>Does your payment flow leave your domain? If yes, treat browser-only tracking as best-effort and plan for CAPI.
A single-page checkout re-initialises the pixel

In single-page applications, if pixel initialisation runs on every virtual page view, the pixel's state resets each time. Advanced matching data gathered earlier in the flow is lost, so the purchase event arrives without the identifiers that make it useful, thin, poorly matched, and sometimes unattributed.
The event fires. It just doesn't carry what it needs, which is why this one is easy to misread as "working."
<t0>The check</t0>Watch the Network tab through the whole checkout. Initialisation should happen once. Events should fire many times.
Deduplication is eating the event

If you run the pixel <t0>and</t0> the Conversions API (which you should), Snapchat deduplicates using <t1>client_dedup_id</t1> (48-hour window) or <t2>transaction_id</t2> (30 days). Two events sharing an identifier are counted once, by design.

It becomes a problem when the browser and server sides disagree about what that identifier is. Get the mapping wrong and you either double-count everything or silently lose one side. Snap's guidance is that non-purchase events map to <t0>client_dedup_id</t0>, and purchase events map to <t1>transaction_id</t1>, and crucially, <t2>the value must match across every path sending that event</t2>.

<t0>Why the identifier you choose matters.</t0> A purchase deduplicated on <t1>transaction_id</t1> stays protected for 30 days. On <t2>client_dedup_id</t2> that protection expires after 48 hours, which is why Snap maps purchases to <t3>transaction_id</t3> and everything else to <t4>client_dedup_id</t4>.
<t0>The check</t0>For one order, capture the identifier the browser sent and the identifier your server sent. They must be identical. Not similar: identical.
Where my own numbers come from

I don't have a large client sample on Snapchat, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. What I have is one store I ran end to end, my own, where the tracking worked, which is the only reason I can talk about what a healthy Snapchat setup produces.

Context that matters, because otherwise these figures flatter me: at 5.69× on $1,452 that's roughly $8,262 in tracked revenue across 1,034 orders, an average order value of about $8. This was a low-ticket product. A $1.40 cost per purchase is a very different achievement at $8 AOV than it would be at $80, and anyone quoting a CPA without an AOV beside it is showing you half a number.
The figures are from a period ending May 2024. I'm dating them rather than presenting them as current.

<t0>What this screenshot does and doesn't prove.</t0> It corroborates the spend (US$1,452.18), the purchase count (1,034), the cost per purchase (US$1.40) and the date range. It also shows 11,076,872 impressions and 242,131 clicks at a 2.19% click rate. It does <t1>not</t1> show ROAS, that figure comes from store-side revenue, not from this view, and you should treat any number you can't see in the frame accordingly.

The reason 1,034 purchases matter for this article isn't the ROAS. It's that a store sending a clean, correctly-named, properly-deduplicated <t0>PURCHASE</t0> event at that volume gives you a reliable baseline for what "working" looks like, and makes it obvious when something has stopped.
What I can't tell you
Two honest limitations, because an article that admits none is usually hiding some.

<t0>I can't give you a frequency ranking from a large sample.</t0> The order above reflects a small number of accounts plus what the failure modes logically imply, a lowercase event name breaks reporting deterministically, so it belongs at the top regardless of how often I have personally seen it. Treat the ranking as a sensible search order, not a statistic.

<t0>Snapchat's interface changes.</t0> Menu paths go stale quickly, which is why the checks above are anchored to the network request and the payload rather than to where a button currently sits. The payload is the thing that's actually true.
The short version
Open the Network tab, filter <t0>tr.snapchat.com</t0>, place a test order.
Confirm the event name is exactly <t0>PURCHASE</t0>, uppercase.
Confirm <t0>transaction_id</t0> is present and unique per order.
Confirm the pixel exists on the page the customer actually lands on.
If checkout leaves your domain, plan for the Conversions API.
If you run pixel and CAPI, confirm the dedup identifier matches exactly on both sides.

If you get through all six and the event still doesn't arrive, the problem is usually not the pixel, it's that the page you're testing isn't the page your customers reach. Go back and complete a real purchase with real money, on a phone, from an ad click. Test orders through a staging link skip precisely the parts that break.

Few explain what happens when two Meta pixels disagree. On one account the second pixel reported purchases that never happened and took 30-40% of daily budget.
Two Meta pixels on Shopify
Can you have two Facebook pixels on one Shopify store?

Technically yes, and several apps exist to make it easy. Whether you should is a different question. Two pixels means two independent records of the same events, and if one is misconfigured you get two conflicting versions of your sales figures with no warning that they disagree.
How do I find all the Facebook pixels installed on my Shopify store?

Check three places: Settings then Customer events for custom pixels, the Facebook and Instagram sales channel, and Online Store then Themes then Edit code searching theme.liquid for fbq or connect.facebook.net. A pixel can be installed in any of these independently.
Should I remove a second Facebook pixel?

If it was installed by a third-party app and you cannot explain what it does that the primary pixel does not, yes. Before removing it, identify which campaigns are optimising toward it, because those campaigns will stop delivering once the pixel is disabled.
Two Meta pixels on one store is not redundancy. It’s two versions of the truth.

Two Meta pixels on one Shopify store does not give you a backup. It gives you <t0>two independent records of the same events</t0>, with nothing keeping them honest. If one is misconfigured, you get two conflicting sales figures and no warning that they disagree, and Meta will happily spend budget optimising toward whichever one is wrong.

Search “multiple Facebook pixels on Shopify” and look at what comes back. App listings selling multi-pixel installation. Vendor guides explaining how to add a second, third, fourth pixel. Tutorials framing it as an advanced tactic.
Almost nothing about what happens when those pixels disagree with each other. That is the article I wish had existed before I audited an account where the answer cost 30 to 40% of the daily budget.
Why people end up with two
Rarely on purpose. The usual routes:
An agency installed one, left, and the next agency installed their own without checking.
A third-party marketing app added its own pixel during setup, often without making it obvious.
Someone pasted a pixel into <t0>theme.liquid</t0> years ago, and the official sales channel was connected later.
Someone read that multiple pixels give you redundancy. They do not.
The through-line is that <t0>nobody involved knew the other pixel existed</t0>. That is what makes this hard to spot: everyone assumes the pixel they installed is the pixel.
What actually goes wrong
They can report different totals, and both look plausible

Two pixels firing under different conditions produce two different purchase counts. Neither looks obviously wrong, because neither is zero. You end up choosing which number to believe based on which dashboard you happened to open.
Campaigns optimise toward whichever pixel they are attached to

This is the expensive one. Campaigns are configured against a specific pixel. If that pixel is reporting inaccurately, those campaigns are optimising toward a signal that does not match reality, and Meta’s delivery system will keep finding more people who trigger that inaccurate signal.
A misconfigured pixel can report purchases that never happened

On the account that prompted this article, the second pixel, installed by a third-party app, was reporting purchases with no corresponding Shopify orders. The campaigns attached to it showed strong ROAS. In Ads Manager they looked like the winners. In the store, they had produced nothing traceable.

Meta reported around 100 orders. Shopify showed 55 to 70. Roughly <t0>PKR 30,000 to 40,000 of a PKR 100,000 daily budget</t0> was going to campaigns optimising toward the pixel that was inventing sales.
Your audiences and optimisation data are split

Even when both pixels are accurate, each one only learns from the traffic it sees. Retargeting audiences are built per pixel. Machine learning is per pixel. Splitting your data across two pixels means both get less of it, which is the opposite of redundancy.
Finding every pixel on your store
Check all three locations. A pixel can be installed in any of them independently, and nothing cross-references them:
<t0>Settings → Customer events</t0>Custom pixels live here, including ones added by apps. Read each one and note its pixel ID.
<t0>The Facebook & Instagram sales channel</t0>The official integration. Note the pixel ID it is connected to.
<t0>Online Store → Themes → Edit code</t0>Search <t1>theme.liquid</t1> for <t2>fbq</t2> and <t3>connect.facebook.net</t3>. Hand-pasted pixels hide here for years.

<t0>Confirm in the browser</t0>Load your store, open DevTools, filter the Network tab for <t1>facebook</t1>, and read the pixel IDs on the outgoing requests. This is the only check that shows what actually runs, rather than what is configured.
If you find more than one distinct pixel ID, you have the situation this article is about.
Removing one safely
<t0>Do not just delete it</t0>

Before disabling a pixel, find out which campaigns are optimising toward it. When I disabled the third-party pixel on that account, <t0>every campaign attached to it stopped delivering.</t0> That was the correct outcome, those campaigns had been running on a conversion signal that was not real, but it is not something to discover by surprise on a client account.
<t0>Map campaigns to pixels</t0>For each active campaign, note which pixel its conversion event is configured against.
<t0>Reconcile each group against your store</t0>Take one settled week. Can you trace the orders each group claims? One group usually cannot be traced at all.
<t0>Keep the pixel you can verify</t0>Usually the official sales channel integration, because you can confirm what installs it and how.
<t0>Warn the client that reported ROAS will fall</t0>It will. Nothing about the business changed; you stopped counting things that were not happening.
<t0>Give it two days, then rebuild</t0>Let clean data accumulate before rebuilding campaigns against the surviving pixel. On that account the picture resolved within a day or two.
The exception worth knowing

There is one legitimate multi-pixel case: a genuine agency or partner arrangement where a second party needs their own conversion data for a defined campaign, and both pixels are known, documented and deliberate.

That is not what most stores have. Most stores have a pixel somebody forgot about, which is a different thing entirely, and the difference is whether anyone can tell you, right now, what each pixel is for.
If you cannot answer that for every pixel on your store, you do not have redundancy. You have an unaudited second opinion that your budget is quietly listening to.
